extracted.intended_audience: practitioners and parties in TTAB trademark oppositions/cancelation proceedings (attorneys, paralegals, litigants)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and practical guidance for conducting discovery in proceedings before the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board (TBMP Chapter 400), including timing, scope, responses, extensions, depositions, privileges, ESI and methods for putting produced documents into the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative production when full production is burdensome
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative samples of documents, including ESI, may be required where full production is unduly burdensome; but a representative sample is inappropriate where full production would not be burdensome (e.g., total of eleven documents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/cases: Frito-Lay North America Inc. v. Princeton Vanguard LLC (100 USPQ2d 1904) (representative samples of documents, including ESI, required for certain requests); Bison Corp. v. Perfecta Chemie B.V. (4 USPQ2d 1718) (representative sample not appropriate where full production small); Sunkist Growers, Inc. v. Benjamin Ansehl Co. (229 USPQ 147) (representative sample of invoices sufficient when too many items); Van Dyk Research Corp. v. Xerox Corp. (181 USPQ 346) (allowed representative samples or site visits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective orders and customer confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Protective agreements/orders can adequately protect trade secret manufacturing and technical information; generally the Board will not require disclosure of customer names or mailing lists unless the issue (e.g., abandonment or first use) makes customer names relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protective order must limit disclosure (e.g., customer names revealed only to applicant's attorneys). For proceedings pending/commenced on/after Aug. 31, 2007, the Board's standard protective order automatically applies absent approved substitute (37 CFR § 2.116(g)). Cases: Red Wing Co. v. J.M. Smucker Co.; Johnston Pump/General Valve Inc. v. Chromalloy American Corp.; Fisons Ltd. v. Capability Brown Ltd.; Neville Chemical Co. v. Lubrizol Corp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privilege assertion requirements and waiver risks
rubrics_metrics.description: A party making a claim of privilege must do so expressly and describe the nature of the withheld information as required by Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(5); disclosure to third parties may waive privilege.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(5). Cases: In re Seagate Technology LLC (attorney-client privilege provides absolute protection absent waiver); Genentech Inc. v. USITC (disclosure to third parties generally constitutes waiver); Red Wing Co. v. J.M. Smucker Co. (party must expressly claim privilege and describe withheld info).

rubrics_metrics.name: Work product protection and the higher burden for mental impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Work product protection is qualified and, absent waiver, may be overcome by a showing of need and undue hardship; a higher showing is required to overcome protection for mental processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(3) and 26(b)(5). Key case: In re Seagate Technology LLC (discussing qualified work product protection and higher burden for mental processes). Other TTAB cases discuss application and limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: ESI not reasonably accessible due to undue burden or cost (Rule 26(b)(2)(B))
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may establish that specific materials (including ESI) sought are not reasonably accessible because of undue burden or cost under Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(2)(B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Frito-Lay North America Inc. v. Princeton Vanguard LLC (opposer established materials not reasonably accessible due to undue burden or costs). Board will consider burden/cost when deciding production of ESI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board-specified discovery schedule; 180-day default discovery period
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board will specify the deadline for a discovery conference, opening and closing dates for discovery, and deadlines for initial and expert disclosures; the discovery period will be set for a period of 180 days (parties may stipulate to shorten).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: 37 CFR § 2.120(a). The trial order setting these deadlines is included with the notice of institution. Parties may stipulate to shorten/extend the period with Board approval or move the Board to extend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery devices limited to the discovery period; no obligation to respond to untimely requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional discovery devices (depositions, interrogatories, requests for production, requests for admission) are available only during the discovery period; a party has no obligation to respond to an untimely request for discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: A party should object to untimely requests. See Smith International v. Olin Corp.; Rhone-Poulenc Industries v. Gulf Oil Corp. Also, service of initial disclosures is a prerequisite to taking discovery in some cases (see other criteria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial disclosures prerequisite to seeking discovery (for cases commenced on/after Nov. 1, 2007)
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases commenced on or after Nov. 1, 2007, a serving party must have already made its initial disclosures before serving written interrogatories, requests for production, or notices of depositions unless waived, stipulated otherwise, or ordered by the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: 37 CFR § 2.120(a)(3). Written discovery may be served concurrently with initial disclosures. Depositions generally cannot be noticed until initial disclosures served (absent stipulation/Board order). Cases: Dating DNA, LLC v. Imagini Holdings; Luster Products Inc. v. Van Zandt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery depositions must be noticed and taken before the close of discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery depositions must be both noticed and taken during the discovery period (unless parties stipulate or the Board orders otherwise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite 37 CFR § 2.120(a)(3) and TBMP § 403.02. A deposition noticed but scheduled after close of discovery may be quashed (National Football League v. DNH Management LLC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time for service of discovery responses: 30 days (plus mailing grace period)
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses to interrogatories, requests for production, and requests for admission must be served within thirty days from the date of service of the discovery request. If served by first-class mail, Express Mail, or overnight courier, five extra days are allowed; no extra days if parties agree to electronic service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: 37 CFR § 2.120(a)(3); Fed. R. Civ. P. 33(b)(2), 34(b)(2)(A), 36(a)(3). See TBMP § 113.05 for mail/delivery rules. Cases: MySpace Inc. v. Donnell Mitchell (timeliness and mailing); Amazon Technologies v. Wax (initial disclosures prerequisite).

rubrics_metrics.name: No priority of right to discovery responses
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that a party served a discovery request first does not give it a right to receive responses before it must respond to its adversary's subsequent requests; each party must respond within the time allowed regardless of sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties are encouraged to initiate discovery early, but timing of responses is governed by rules not sequence. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(d) and cases cited (Miss America Pageant v. Petite Productions; Giant Food v. Standard Terry Mills).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of failing to respond: forfeiture and motions to reopen
rubrics_metrics.description: A party that fails to respond to interrogatories or document requests within the allowed time and cannot show excusable neglect may be found to have forfeited its right to object; for requests for admissions, the party may move to reopen time to respond (excusable neglect) or move to withdraw/amend admissions under Fed. R. Civ. P. 36(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: No Fear Inc. v. Rule (Board's discretion regarding forfeiture); Envirotech Corp. v. Compagnie Des Lampes; Luehrmann v. Kwik Kopy Corp. (excusable neglect contexts). Parties should attempt good faith efforts to determine reasons before moving to compel. See MacMillan Bloedel Ltd. v. Arrow-M Corp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of objections: merits objections vs privilege/confidentiality objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections that go to the merits of a discovery request include irrelevance, overbreadth, vagueness/ambiguity, burdensomeness/oppression, or not likely to lead to admissible evidence. Objections based on privilege, confidentiality or attorney work product do not go to the merits but to the characteristic of the information sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merits objections can result in nonproduction if sustained; privilege/work product objections must be asserted properly and may be subject to in camera review or other procedures to protect confidentiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensions of discovery and response times: stipulation, motion, or Board order
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery period or time to respond to discovery may be extended upon stipulation of the parties approved by the Board, upon a motion granted by the Board, or by order of the Board. Resetting closing date for discovery reschedules pretrial disclosure deadlines and testimony periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: 37 CFR § 2.120(a)(2) and § 2.121(a). If a motion for extension is denied, the discovery period may remain as originally set or as reset. See TBMP §§ 501.03 and 509 for stipulations and motions to extend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and filing requirements for stipulations to reschedule deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: When parties stipulate to reschedule deadlines (pretrial disclosures, testimony periods, or close of discovery), the stipulation should be presented in the form used in a trial order, signed by the parties, or a motion in that form signed by one party including a statement that every other party has agreed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: 37 CFR § 2.121(d). Filing the stipulation in the correct form avoids procedural defects and ensures the Board will reset related deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of extension on expert disclosure deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: When the discovery period is extended by stipulation or Board order, the Board ordinarily will reset the deadline for expert disclosure; however, if expert disclosure time has passed and disclosures were already served or parties do not intend to use experts, the Board may not reset that deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board will commonly reschedule expert disclosures because expert-related discovery is expected to occur within the discovery period. See TBMP § 403.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere delay in initiating discovery not good cause; improper delay in responding may justify extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere delay in initiating discovery does not ordinarily constitute good cause for extending the discovery period. Conversely, if a party delays responding or responds improperly such that the propounding party loses opportunity for follow-up discovery, that delay or improper response constitutes good cause for an extension (at least for the propounding party).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: National Football League v. DNH Management LLC (denial where written discovery served only on final day); Luehrmann v. Kwik Kopy Corp. (no reason given). For delays causing lost follow-up discovery see Miss America Pageant v. Petite Productions; Neville Chemical Co. v. Lubrizol Corp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to serve initial requests early to allow follow-up discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party wants an opportunity to take follow-up discovery after receiving responses, it must serve its initial requests early in the discovery period so there is time to prepare and serve additional requests before discovery closes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See TBMP § 403.05(a) and TBMP § 403.04. Strategic note: combine timing considerations with the 30-day response period and deposition timing when planning discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produced documents generally cannot be made of record by notice of reliance alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents obtained from another party through disclosure or Rule 34 production may not be made of record by notice of reliance alone, except to the extent they qualify as printed publications or official records under 37 CFR § 2.122(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 CFR § 2.122(e) sets requirements for printed publications/official records (identify source/date/pages, indicate relevance, and attach copy/authenticated copy). For other produced documents, parties should use stipulation or other methods (see separate criterion). See TBMP § 704.09 for full discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods to make produced documents of record
rubrics_metrics.description: If produced documents do not qualify for notice of reliance under § 2.122(e), they may be made of record by: (1) stipulation that any party may introduce by notice of reliance documents produced by any other party; (2) serving requests for admission of genuineness (with exhibits attached) during discovery and later filing notice of reliance on the admission and exhibit; (3) taking a discovery deposition, marking produced documents as exhibits and having the witness identify them, then submitting the deposition and exhibits under notice of reliance; or (4) combining a request for production with a notice of deposition that asks the deponent to bring the documents to the deposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing: these methods require that the request for production or deposition be served/taken while discovery is still open (e.g., combined request/deposition normally must be served at least 35 days before close due to 30-day response + 5-day mail rules). Examples: ProQuest v. Island; Kohler Co. v. Baldwin Hardware Corp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery depositions: courtesy scheduling and duty to cooperate
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a deposing party may notice a deposition unilaterally, parties should attempt to schedule depositions by agreement to avoid conflicts; parties have a duty to cooperate in discovery scheduling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See TBMP § 404.01 and § 408. Cases: Sunrider Corp. v. Raats (duty to cooperate in scheduling); Luehrmann v. Kwik Kopy Corp. (parties ordered to work out mutually agreeable schedule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may be deposed and Board permission limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally any person (party or non-party) may be deposed by oral questions; however, Board permission (leave) is required without stipulation if the proposed deposition would result in more than ten discovery depositions being taken by the plaintiffs or by the defendants, or if the deponent has already been deposed, or if the deponent is confined in prison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(a) and TBMP § 404.02. A nonparty witness residing in the U.S. may be deposed by subpoena (Rule 45) or on notice if the nonparty agrees voluntarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place and manner of depositions (persons residing in the U.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery deposition of a natural person shall be taken in the federal judicial district where the person resides or is regularly employed, or at any place the parties stipulate; depositions may be oral or on written questions under 37 CFR § 2.124.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: 37 CFR § 2.120(b). Note: Board proceedings do not follow the district-court rule requiring plaintiff's availability in the district where suit is brought (Jain v. Ramparts Inc.). See TBMP § 404.03 for written-question procedures.
